analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal estate tax on the largest inherited fortunes.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and never received a vote before the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have permanently eliminated the federal estate tax, which is levied only on very large inheritances, along with the tax on transfers that skip a generation. It would have kept a separate gift tax but with a lower rate schedule and a $10 million lifetime exemption, adjusted for inflation. The bill was introduced in March 2018, referred to the Ways and Means Committee, and never advanced further.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to the largest fortunes — the small share of estates large enough to owe the tax. In 2018 an individual could pass roughly $11 million to heirs tax-free, so the tax touched only a tiny fraction of estates, concentrated among the wealthiest households. Wealth-transfer planning that depends on the tax's existence would be disrupted.

how_it_helps.text: Permanently repeals the estate tax, ending the 40% tax on inherited estates above the exemption threshold.
Repeals the generation-skipping transfer tax, which applies when wealth passes directly to grandchildren, allowing such transfers without an additional layer of tax.
Keeps the gift tax but lowers its top rate to 35% and sets a $10 million lifetime exemption, so large fortunes could be given away during life at a reduced cost.

analysis.who_pays: The federal treasury, and by extension all other taxpayers, through roughly $100 billion in lost revenue over a decade. Because the tax falls almost entirely on the largest estates, the benefit would concentrate at the very top while the revenue loss is shared by everyone.

drawbacks.text: Repeal would eliminate a progressive tax that falls only on the largest inheritances, converting that revenue into larger deficits or higher taxes elsewhere.

The bill's pitch targets family farms and small businesses, but the estate tax already exempts millions per person, so very few farms or small firms actually owe it; the direct gain goes to the largest estates.
The bill retains the gift tax at reduced rates and with a $10 million exemption, leaving a residual transfer tax that wealthy families would still need to plan around.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits are real but narrow: heirs to multimillion-dollar estates would keep significantly more. The costs — lost federal revenue that would otherwise be raised from other taxpayers or borrowed — fall broadly on everyone, while very few family farms or small businesses would see any change. As designed, this is a tax cut aimed at the top of the wealth distribution, not at ordinary working families.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up, so it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jason Smith introduced the bill on March 29, 2018, with Rep. Sanford Bishop and Rep. Kristi Noem as original sponsors, and it attracted 11 cosponsors (10 Republicans, 1 Democrat).
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the day it was introduced.
The action history shows no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action; the bill received no vote in either chamber before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the estate tax stayed in place: the federal treasury kept the revenue, and the largest estates continued to pay the tax. The bill's intended beneficiaries — heirs to the largest fortunes — gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The federal treasury and largest estates' taxpayers

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Republican: 10 of the bill's 11 cosponsors were Republicans, with one Democrat (Rep. Bishop of Georgia), and the bill never attracted broader action in the GOP-controlled House.

industries.industry: Heirs to the largest fortunes (top ~0.2% of estates)
industries.note: Repeal would have let the largest inherited estates escape a 40% tax, while the lost revenue would be borne by deficits or other taxpayers. The bill's benefit is concentrated precisely where the tax currently applies: multimillion-dollar estates.

industries.industry: Estate planning and wealth advisory firms
industries.note: A large share of trust and estate planning exists to minimize estate tax exposure; permanent repeal would shrink that business. Their interest ran against the bill, alongside preserving the tax that funds the treasury.
These are the bill's stated beneficiaries, but the tax's per-person exemption already shelters most farms and small firms, so few would owe the tax before or after repeal.
Repeal would remove tens of billions of dollars in revenue over a decade, worsening deficits or requiring offsets from other taxpayers.
